verses.text: Philocrates,{a} the account of our meeting with Eleazar,{b} the high priest of the Jews, is worth telling. You have set great store by hearing it, by my going over each point and explaining why we were sent and for what purpose, and so I have tried to set it out plainly for you, knowing how much you love learning,

which is the highest good a person can have: to keep learning, and to keep taking in something further, whether through histories or through living the events oneself. For in this way a pure disposition is formed in the soul. It takes up what is finest, and, turning to piety, the most commanding thing of all, it governs itself by a rule that never misleads.

We were set on examining divine matters with care, and so we offered ourselves for an embassy to the man I mentioned. He is held in the highest honor for his nobility and good name by his citizens and by others, and he has won very great benefits for those with him and for his fellow citizens elsewhere. Our purpose was the translation of the divine law, since it is written among them on skins in Hebrew letters.

We carried this out eagerly, once we had found an opening with the king about the people who had been moved to Egypt from Judea{c} by the king’s father, who had been the first to take possession of the city{d} and to take over Egypt.{e} It is worth telling you this as well.

I am convinced that you lean strongly toward reverence and toward the character of people who live by the holy law, and so you will gladly hear what we intend to tell. You have only lately come to us from the island,{f} and you wish to hear whatever helps to renew the soul.
I also sent you an account earlier of matters I thought worth remembering, which we received from the high priests of Egypt, that most learned land, about the people of the Jews.

You love learning, and so it is right to share with you whatever can benefit the mind. It is right to share it with all who are like you, and much more with you, who hold such an honest conviction. You are not only my brother by kinship in character; you are also the same as I am in your eagerness for what is good.

For the charm of gold, or any other costly possession prized by the vain, does not bring the same benefit as the discipline of education and the care taken over it. But so that we do not become tiresome by dragging out the preliminaries, I will go back to the continuous course of the account.

Demetrius of Phalerum,{g} who had been put in charge of the king’s library, was given large and varied sums in order to gather together, if he could, all the books in the inhabited world. By purchases and by copying, he carried the king’s purpose as far toward its end as was in his power.

We were present when he was asked, “About how many tens of thousands of books are there?” He said, “More than two hundred thousand,{h} O king. I will take pains, within a short time, to bring the rest up to five hundred thousand.{i} I have been told that the laws of the Jews are also worth copying and worth a place in your library.”

“What is stopping you from doing this?” the king asked. “Everything you need has been put at your disposal.” Demetrius said, “They need translation. They use letters of their own, as the Egyptians have their own arrangement of letters, and they have a language of their own as well. They are assumed to use Syriac,{j} but that is not so; theirs is a different kind.” The king took in each point and gave orders that a letter should go to the Jews’ high priest, so that what had been said might be carried out.

The city is Alexandria, named for Alexander the Great (Greek *Alexandros*, “defender of men”).

verses.text: I thought the moment had come to press what I had often asked of Sosibius{a} of Tarentum{b} and Andreas,{c} the chiefs of the bodyguard: the release of those who had been moved out of Judea by the king’s father. For that king had gone through all of Coele-Syria{d} and Phoenicia,{e} using his success together with courage. Some people he deported, and others he took captive, bringing everything under his hand by fear. In the course of this he carried off to Egypt about a hundred thousand people{f} from the land of the Jews.

Of these he armed about thirty thousand{g} picked men and settled them in the country in the garrisons. (Many had already come in earlier, with the Persian{h}, and others before them had been sent as allies to fight the king of the Ethiopians{i} with Psammetichus.{j} But those were not as many as the ones Ptolemy{k} son of Lagus{l} brought over.)

As I said, he chose those who were best in age and outstanding in strength and armed them. The rest of the crowd, older and younger and women as well, he left in servitude. This was not what he really wanted in his heart; he was overruled by his soldiers because of the services they had rendered in the struggles of war. When we found a pretext for their release, as I have already explained, we spoke to the king in these words.

“It would be absurd, O king, to be proved wrong by the facts themselves. A body of law lies before all the Jews, and we intend not only to copy it but to translate it. What reason could we give for sending it, while great numbers of the same people are in servitude in your kingdom? No, with a perfect and generous spirit, release those who are held in misery. For the God who gave them their law is guiding your kingdom, as I have found by inquiry.{m}

They worship the God who oversees all things and created them, whom all people worship, and we as well, O king, though under other names, Zeus and Dios.{n} The first people to name him this way did so fittingly: that by which everything receives life and comes into being is the guide and lord of all. You surpass all people in the brightness of your mind, so release those who are held in servitude.”

After a short time, as we prayed in our hearts to God that he would shape the king’s mind toward the release of them all (for the human race is God’s creation, and God changes and turns it as he wishes; so in many and various ways I called on the one who rules the heart, that he might be compelled, as I asked, to do it),

for I had great hope, as I made my plea for the rescue of human beings, that God would bring about what was asked. What people believe they are doing in holiness, for justice and the care of good works, is directed in its deeds and plans by God, who rules over all.

The king looked up, glanced at me with a cheerful face, and said, “About how many tens of thousands do you think they will number?” Andreas, who was standing by, answered, “A little over a hundred thousand.” “A small thing indeed,” the king said, “that Aristeas{o} asks of us.” Sosibius and some of those present said, “It is also worthy of your generosity to present their release to the most high God as an offering of thanks. You have been honored supremely by the one who rules all things, and made more glorious than your ancestors. So if you make very great thank offerings, it is fitting for you.”

The king was greatly delighted. He ordered that the soldiers’ pay be increased, that twenty drachmas{p} be paid for each person, and that an order be issued about this, with the registrations made at once. He acted with generous eagerness, since God was bringing to completion our whole purpose and forcing the king to ransom not only the men who had arrived along with his father’s army but also anyone who had been there before or was brought into the kingdom afterward. They reckoned the payment at more than four hundred talents (about 30,000 pounds of silver).{q}
I think it is useful to include a copy of the order as well. The king’s generosity will be far clearer and more obvious, since God was strengthening him to bring rescue to so many multitudes.

It read as follows. “By order of the king: All those who served in the army with our father in the regions of Syria{r} and Phoenicia, and who entered the land of the Jews and gained possession of Jewish persons and brought them to the city and the country, or sold them to others, and likewise anyone who had them earlier or has had them brought in since, are to release them at once, for money. Each owner is to receive twenty drachmas for each person: soldiers as an addition to their pay, and the others from the royal bank.

We consider that these people were taken captive against our father’s wish and contrary to what is right, and that, because of the recklessness of soldiers, their land was laid waste and the removal of the Jews to Egypt took place. The gain the soldiers made in the field was enough. Therefore the oppression of human beings is altogether unreasonable.

We acknowledge that justice is owed to all people, and much more to those who are wrongly oppressed. We seek in every way what is right toward justice and toward piety for all. We therefore order that all Jewish persons who are in servitude anywhere in the kingdom, in whatever way, are to be released by those who hold them, on receipt of the stated sum, and that no one is to handle these matters with malicious delay. The registrations are to be made within three days from the day this order is posted, before those appointed for the purpose, and the persons are to be produced at once.

We judge that this will serve us and our affairs. Whoever wishes to report those who disobey may do so, on the understanding that he will gain control of the one found guilty. The property of such people will be taken into the royal treasury.”

The order was brought in to be read to the king, and it contained all of this except the words “and anyone who had them earlier or has had them brought in since.” The king added this himself, in his generosity and greatness of spirit. He also ordered that the whole sum of the payments be divided up among the officers’ attendants in the divisions and the royal bankers.

So it was decided and confirmed within seven days. The payment came to more than six hundred sixty talents (about 49,500 pounds of silver).{s} Many nursing infants were set free with their mothers, too. When the king was asked whether the twenty drachmas would be paid for these as well, he ordered that this too be done, carrying out completely what he had decided.

verses.text: When this had been accomplished, the king ordered Demetrius to submit a proposal about the copying of the Jewish books. Everything under these kings was handled by written orders and with great care, and nothing was done carelessly or at random. For this reason I have included the text of the proposal and copies of the letters, the number of the gifts sent, and the workmanship of each, since every one of them stood out for its lavishness and skill. This is a copy of the proposal.

“To the great king, from Demetrius. You gave orders, O king, that the books still missing to complete the library be gathered in, and that those that have fallen into disrepair receive proper restoration. I have given careful attention to these matters, and I now report the following to you.

The books of the law of the Jews are missing, along with a few others. They happen to be written in Hebrew letters and language, but they have been set down rather carelessly and not as they really stand, as those who know them report; for they have never had the king’s care.

It is necessary that these too be in your possession in an exact form, since this legislation is wiser and unspoiled, as one would expect of a divine law. For that reason, writers, poets, and the whole crowd of historians have kept their distance from mentioning these books and the men who have lived and still live by them, because the thinking in them is pure and solemn, as Hecataeus of Abdera{a} says.

If it seems good to you, O king, a letter will be written to the high priest in Jerusalem{b} to send elderly men whose lives have been the best, experienced in their own law, six from each tribe. We will then examine what the majority agree on, obtain an accurate translation, and set it down clearly, in a way worthy of the matter and of your purpose. May you prosper always.”

When this proposal had been presented, the king ordered a letter to be written to Eleazar about these matters, reporting also the release of the captives that had taken place. He gave, too, for the making of mixing bowls, cups, a table, and bowls for pouring offerings, fifty talents’ weight of gold (about 3,750 pounds){c} and seventy talents of silver (about 5,250 pounds), along with a great quantity of precious stones. He ordered the keepers of the treasure chests to let the craftsmen choose whichever stones they preferred. He also gave coined money for sacrifices and other needs, nearly a hundred talents (about 7,500 pounds of silver).
I will tell you about the workmanship once I have gone through the copies of the letters. The king’s letter was in this form.

“King Ptolemy sends Eleazar the high priest greetings, and wishes him health. It has happened that many Jews have been settled in our country, having been carried off from Jerusalem by the Persians during the time they ruled, and that others came to Egypt with our father as captives.

Of these our father enrolled many in the army on higher pay. He also judged those who were there earlier to be trustworthy, built forts, and handed these over to them, so that the nation of the Egyptians would be afraid because of them. Now that we have taken over the kingdom, we deal with everyone more kindly, and much more so with your fellow citizens.

We have set free more than a hundred thousand captives, giving their owners the silver they were owed, and putting right whatever was done wrongly through the rush of the crowds. We have judged that this was a pious thing to do, and we offer it in thanks to the greatest God, who has held our realm in peace and raised it to the height of glory throughout the whole inhabited world. We have placed those in the prime of life in the army, and those who are able to be near us and are worthy of trust at court we have set over our affairs.

We wish to show favor both to these people and to all the Jews in the world, and to those who come after them. We have therefore decided that your law be translated into Greek letters from the Hebrew letters, as they are called among you, so that these books too may be in our library with the other royal books.

You will do well, and in a manner worthy of our eagerness, to choose elderly men who have lived good lives, who are experienced in the law and able to translate it, six from each tribe, so that agreement may be found among the larger number, since the inquiry concerns weighty matters. For we believe that when this is finished we will win great fame.

We have sent Andreas, of the chiefs of the bodyguard, and Aristeas, who are held in honor among us, to talk with you. They are bringing first offerings of dedicated gifts for the temple, and a hundred talents of silver (about 7,500 pounds) for sacrifices and other needs. If you write to us about whatever you wish, you will please us and do something worthy of friendship, and what you choose will be carried out as quickly as possible. Farewell.”

Eleazar answered this letter, in suitable terms. It went like this: “Eleazar, high priest, to King Ptolemy, his true friend: greetings. May you be well, and the queen Arsinoe,{d} your sister, and your children; it would be as we wish. We are well also.

When we received your letter, we rejoiced greatly over your purpose and your good plan. We gathered the whole community and read it aloud to them, so that they would learn how devout you are toward our God. We also showed them the gifts you sent: bowls, twenty of gold and thirty of silver, with five mixing bowls, and a table for dedication, and a hundred talents of silver (about 7,500 pounds) for bringing sacrifices and for repairs of whatever the temple needs,

Greek *Hierosolyma*, from Hebrew *Yerushalayim*, perhaps “foundation of peace.”

verses.text: for we will obey in everything that is to your advantage, even if it goes against our nature, since this is a sign of friendship and affection. You, too, have done great and unforgettable good to our citizens in many ways.

Immediately, then, we offered sacrifices for you, for your sister, your children, and your friends. The whole community prayed that all you intend may always come to you, that God, who rules over all, may keep your kingdom safe in peace and glory, and that the copying of the holy law may be carried out to your benefit and in safety.

In the presence of everyone we chose good and fine elderly men, six from each tribe, and we have sent them with the law. You will do well, righteous king, to give orders that when the copying of the books is finished, the men are brought back to us again in safety. Farewell.”

These are the men. From the first tribe: Joseph, Hezekiah, Zechariah, John, Hezekiah, Elisha.{a} From the second: Judah, Simon, Samuel, Adaeus, Mattathias, Eschlemias.{b} From the third: Nehemiah, Joseph, Theodosius, Baseas, Ornias, Dakis.{c}

From the fourth: Jonathan, Abaeus, Elisha, Hananiah, Chabrias, Chelkias (this last name is doubtful in the Greek).{d} From the fifth: Isaac, Jacob, Jesus, Sabbataeus, Simon, Levi.{e} From the sixth: Judah, Joseph, Simon, Zechariah, Samuel, Selemias.{f}

From the seventh: Sabbataeus, Zedekiah, Jacob, Isaac, Jesias, Natthaeus.{g} From the eighth: Theodosius, Jason, Jesus, Theodotus, John, Jonathan.{h} From the ninth: Theophilus, Abram, Arsamus, Jason, Endemias, Daniel.{i}

From the tenth: Jeremiah, Eleazar, Zechariah, Baneas, Elisha, Dathaeus.{j} From the eleventh: Samuel, Joseph, Judah, Jonathan, Chabeu, Dositheus.{k} From the twelfth: Isael, John, Theodosius, Arsamus, Abietes, Ezekiel.{l} In all they were seventy-two.

Such was the reply that Eleazar and those with him made to the king’s letter. I will now do as I promised and describe the works of craftsmanship. They were completed with outstanding skill, since the king contributed lavishly and looked in on the craftsmen at every stage. So they could not overlook anything or finish anything carelessly. First I will explain to you what concerns the table.
The king was eager to make the piece enormous in its measurements. He ordered inquiry to be made of people in that region about how large the table already standing in the temple in Jerusalem was.

When they told him the measurements, he asked whether he should also make a larger one. Some of the priests, and others, said that nothing prevented it. He said he wished to make it five times the size, but he was afraid it might become useless for the services.

For he did not want what came from him merely to sit in that place. He would be far more pleased if the proper services were carried out correctly on the pieces he had made, by those to whom that duty fell.

“The earlier pieces are small,” he said, “not for lack of gold; it appears that they were made to these measures for some reason. If there had been an instruction to make them larger, nothing would have been withheld. So what has been rightly done must not be overstepped or set aside.”

He ordered them to use as much variety of craftsmanship as possible, planning everything with dignity and having a fine natural sense for the expressiveness of things. Where nothing was prescribed in writing, he ordered them to make it beautiful; where it was prescribed in writing, the measures were to follow it.

They made it two cubits (3 feet) long and a cubit and a half (27 inches) high,{m} working it in tested gold, solid all the way through. I mean that the gold was not wrapped around some other material; the hammered plate itself was joined together.

They made a rim a palm (about 3 inches) wide{n} all around. The moldings were twisted, carved in relief with a pattern of cords, and wonderful in their run when seen from the three sides, for the piece was three-cornered.

On each side the design of the work had the same arrangement, so that whichever side was turned, the appearance was the same. With the molding laid along the rim, the slope toward the table itself held the pattern of beauty, and the outward slope faced the view of the person approaching.

So the ridge between the two slopes came to a sharp edge, standing up, as we said, because it was built three-cornered whichever side was turned. Settings of costly stones lay in it between the cords, one beside another, with a weaving that no one could imitate.
All were held through drilled holes by gold pins for security. At the corners, clasps drew them tight to hold them together.

At the sides, around the rim, on the part facing upward, a pattern of eggs was made with stones set in it, with a design that drew the eye in continuous fluted reliefs, set close together all around the table.

Beneath the stone-set pattern of eggs the craftsmen made a wreath of every kind of fruit, standing out clearly in relief: bunches of grapes and heads of grain, with dates, apples, olives, pomegranates, and the like. They cut the stones to the shapes of these fruits, each kind in its own color, and bound them in the gold, all around the whole edge of the table.

After the arrangement of the wreath, the same pattern was made as for the eggs, and the rest of the fluting and carving was done in the same way. This was because the table was made usable on both sides, whichever side was lifted, so that the placing of the moldings and of the rim was also at the end where the legs were.

They made a solid plate four fingers (about 3 inches) thick{o} across the whole width of the table, so that the legs could be set into it, fastened with pins and clasps at the rim. That way, whichever side was lifted would be the one in use. This can be seen on the surface, since the piece was made to be used either way up.
On the table itself they made a meander in relief, with costly stones standing out in the middle of it, of various kinds: carbuncles and emeralds, onyx, and other kinds outstanding in beauty.

After the arrangement of the meander lay a latticework, wonderful to see, making a diamond pattern in the middle. On it a crystal stone and what is called electrum{p} were set in relief, making a sight that no one could imitate.
They made the legs with capitals shaped like lilies, with the lilies bending back beneath the table, and the face toward the inside had its petals standing straight.

The base on which the leg rested on the floor was a palm (about 3 inches) high on every side and made of stone, set like a plinth in appearance, and eight fingers (about 6 inches) wide. On it rested the whole plate of the leg.{q}

They made ivy growing out of the stone, interwoven with acanthus, winding with a vine around the leg, with clusters of grapes, which were also worked in stone, up to the top. The same arrangement was used on all four legs. Everything was made so lifelike and fitted so well that the skill of the craftsmen matched the real thing exactly. Even when a breath of wind stirred the air, the leaves would move, since everything was modeled on the living thing.

They made the top of the table in three parts, like a three-leaved panel, fitted to one another with dovetail joints through the thickness of the piece, and they made the joining of the seams so that it could not be seen or found. The thickness of the whole table was not less than half a cubit (about 9 inches), so that the whole piece was worth many talents.

For the king had decided not to add anything to the size, and what would have had to be spent on making larger pieces he gave instead for these, in greater amount. According to his plan, everything was completed wonderfully and notably, inimitable in its craftsmanship and outstanding in beauty.
Of the mixing bowls, two were made of gold. They had a scale pattern that ran from the base to the middle, and between the scales stones were set with great skill.

Then came a meander a cubit (18 inches) high, with its relief in varied stonework, showing with beauty the painstaking labor of the craft. Above this was fluting, and above that an interweaving of diamond shapes with a net-like face, all the way up to the mouth.

In the middle were little shields of stones, one beside another, each of a different kind, not less than four fingers (about 3 inches) across, and they filled out the clear beauty of the piece. On the rim of the body a relief of lilies with honeysuckle ornaments, and twisting cords of grape clusters, were modeled all around.

The gold ones had this construction, and each held more than two measures (more than 20 gallons).{r} The silver ones had a smooth surface that served as a mirror, wonderful for this purpose, so that anything brought near was reflected more clearly than in ordinary mirrors.

It is not possible to describe what was accomplished for the sake of lifelike effect. When the pieces were finished and set one beside another (I mean first a silver bowl, then a gold one, then silver and gold again), the effect on the eye was altogether indescribable, and those who came to look could not tear themselves away, because of the dazzling light and the pleasure of the sight.

The effect of the surface was varied. Those who looked at the gold work felt a spell of wonder, as the mind turned continually to each piece of craft. And when someone wished to look at the arrangement of the silver pieces, everything shone around from every side, wherever one stood, and increased the delight of those who watched. So the many arts used in them were beyond description.

The gold cups they engraved with wreaths of vine in the middle, and around the rims they wove a wreath in relief of ivy, myrtle, and olive, setting costly stones in them. The rest of the work they finished in different ways, all of them striving to add to the king’s glory.
All in all, no work of such expense and craftsmanship existed in the royal treasuries or anywhere else. The king took no small care, since he loved glory in fine things.

He often put aside public business and sat attentively beside the craftsmen, so that they would finish the works in a way fitting to the place to which they were being sent. So everything was done with dignity, and worthy of the king who sent it and of the high priest who presided over the place.

The number of stones was lavish, and they were large, not fewer than five thousand, and all were of the highest craftsmanship, so that the gift of the stones and the work of the craftsmen were worth five times the gold.

In order: Nehemiah (*Nechemyah*), “Yahweh comforts”; Joseph; Theodosius, a Greek name meaning “gift of God”; Baseas, Ornias, and Dakis, whose meanings are uncertain.

In order: Jonathan (*Yehonatan*), “Yahweh has given”; Abaeus, meaning uncertain; Elisha; Hananiah (*Chananyah*), “Yahweh has been gracious”; Chabrias, a Greek name, perhaps “graceful”; Chelkias, perhaps for Hilkiah (*Chilqiyah*), “Yahweh is my portion.”

In order: Isaac (*Yitschaq*), “he laughs”; Jacob (*Ya’aqov*), “he grasps the heel” or “may God protect”; Jesus, the Greek form of *Yeshua*, Joshua, “Yahweh saves”; Sabbataeus, “born on the Sabbath”; Simon; Levi (*Levi*), “joined.”
Selemias, perhaps for Shelemiah (*Shelemyah*), “Yahweh repays” or “Yahweh is peace.” The other names are explained above.
In order: Sabbataeus; Zedekiah (*Tsidqiyah*), “Yahweh is my righteousness”; Jacob; Isaac; Jesias, perhaps for Isaiah or Joshua; Natthaeus, meaning uncertain.
Jason, a Greek name meaning “healer,” often used by Jews in place of Joshua; Theodotus, a Greek name meaning “given by God.”

In order: Theophilus, “friend of God”; Abram (*Avram*), “exalted father”; Arsamus, a name of Persian or Semitic origin, meaning uncertain; Jason; Endemias, meaning uncertain; Daniel (*Daniyel*), “God is my judge.”
Jeremiah (*Yirmeyahu*), “Yahweh lifts up” or “Yahweh loosens”; Baneas, perhaps for Benaiah (*Benayahu*), “Yahweh has built”; Dathaeus, meaning uncertain.
Chabeu, meaning uncertain; Dositheus, a Greek name meaning “gift of God.”
Isael, perhaps for Israel (*Yisra’el*), “he struggles with God”; Abietes, perhaps for Abiah (*Aviyah*), “Yahweh is my father”; Ezekiel (*Yechezqel*), “God strengthens.”

Greek: a “palm,” one-fourth of a cubit’s measure of six palms, taken here as about 3 inches (7.5 cm).
Greek: “four fingers”; a finger is taken as about three-quarters of an inch (1.9 cm).

verses.text: I thought a record of these things was also necessary, and so I have made them plain to you. Next comes the account of our trip to Eleazar; before that, I will describe the lie of the whole country. When we reached those parts, we saw the city lying in the middle of all Judea, on a mountain rising to a great height.

On the summit the temple had been built, splendid to look at. It had three enclosing walls, each more than seventy cubits (about 105 feet) in size,{a} and the breadth and length matched the design of the house itself. Everything was built with a grandeur and lavishness that surpassed all else.
The doorway, the fastenings around it along the doorposts, and the strength of the lintels made it plain that money had been spent without stint.

The curtain was made very much like the doorway in every respect. Because the air moved beneath it, the woven fabric was kept in constant motion, as the billowing, which began at the floor, stretched all the way up to the top. The sight was pleasant and hard to turn away from.

The altar was built to suit the place, and the sacrifices that were burned up by fire were offered on it. The approach to the altar was laid out for good order, and the priests who served were covered down to the ankles in tunics of fine linen.

The house faces east, with its back to the west. The whole floor is paved with stone and slopes toward suitable places so that water can be carried off, which is needed to wash away the blood of the sacrifices; for tens of thousands of animals are brought in on feast days.

The supply of water never fails. A spring with abundant flow wells up naturally from within, and there are also wonderful and indescribable reservoirs underground, reaching, as they showed us, five stadia (about 3,000 feet) around the foundation of the temple.{b} From each of these run countless pipes, where the streams join together on every side.

All of these were lined with lead on the floor and the wall, and a great quantity of plaster had been poured over them, everything done with care. There were many openings at the base, invisible to everyone except those who perform the service, so that at a signal all the blood of the great mass of sacrifices that collects can be washed away.

I will describe the construction of the reservoirs as I myself became convinced of it. They led me out of the city more than four stadia (about half a mile), and at one place they told me to bend down and listen to the noise of the waters meeting. In this way the size of the vessels became clear to me, as I have said.

The service of the priests is in every respect unsurpassed in strength and in orderly, silent arrangement. All work hard of their own accord, though it is very toilsome, and each one cares for what has been assigned to him. They serve without pause, some bringing wood, others oil, others fine flour, others spices, and others burning the flesh of the offerings, using exceptional strength.

They take hold of the calves’ legs with both hands (each calf weighs about two talents or more, about 150 pounds){c} and fling them up to a wonderful height, one with each hand, and never miss the placing. The sheep and goats, too, are remarkable for weight and fat. Those in charge always choose animals without blemish and outstanding in plumpness, and so what I have described is accomplished.
A place is set aside for their rest, where those who are taking a break sit. When that happens, those of the others who have stopped rise up eagerly, with no one giving orders for the service.

Complete silence prevails, so that one would suppose no human being was present in the place, though the ministers there number about seven hundred, besides a great crowd of those bringing offerings. Yet everything is carried out with reverence, in a way worthy of great divinity.

It caused us great astonishment when we saw Eleazar at his service, with the splendor of his dress and the glory that comes from the robe he wears and the stones about him. Golden bells hang around his ankle-length robe, giving out a distinctive sound of melody, and beside each of these are little pomegranates embroidered with flowers, wonderful in color.

He was girded with a splendid belt of unusual make, woven through with the loveliest colors. On his chest he wears what is called the breastpiece, in which twelve stones of different kinds are fastened, set in gold, with the names of the tribal leaders in the order established from the beginning. Each one flashes out the natural color proper to it, beyond description.

He wears on his head the so-called turban, and on that the inimitable headband, the consecrated royal emblem, with the name of God{d} stamped in sacred letters on a gold plate in the middle of his brow. He is full of glory, since he was judged worthy of these things for the services.

The sight of all this brings fear and confusion, so that one thinks one has come into another world outside this one. I assure you that every person who comes near to see the things I have described will be filled with amazement and indescribable wonder, his mind changed by the holy arrangement of every part.

To get to know everything, we climbed to the citadel beside the city and looked around. It stands in a very high place, secured by many towers, which were built up to the top with long stones, as we learned, to guard the places around the temple,

so that if there should be an attack, an uprising, or an assault by enemies, no one could force a way into the enclosures around the house. Arrow-shooting engines stood on the towers of the citadel, and engines of various kinds, and the place lay above the enclosures I have described,

and the towers were guarded by the most trustworthy men, who had given great proofs of loyalty to their country. They had no authority to leave the citadel except on feast days, and then only some of them, and they allowed no one to come in.

They were very strict even when an order came through the one in command to admit certain people to see the place, as happened in our own case. They barely admitted the two of us, unarmed, to observe the sacrifices.

They said that this was also confirmed by oaths. All of them had sworn, under the compulsion of their religion, to keep the rule: since there were five hundred of them, no more than five persons could be let in together. For the whole guarding of the temple is the citadel, and whoever is in charge of it is made secure in this way against the dangers I have mentioned.

The extent of the city is proportionate, with a circuit of about forty stadia (about 4½ miles), as far as one can estimate. The towers are arranged like the rows of a theater, and passages can be seen, some lower down and some above, with ways through them. The ground slopes because the city is built on a mountain, and stairways lead up to the passages.

Some people take their road on the upper level and others beneath, and they keep well away from the road, because of those who are in states of purification, so that they touch nothing they should not.

It was not without reason that the first builders laid out the city in fitting proportion; they planned it wisely. The country is large and fine. Some of it is plain, the part around what is called Samaria{e} and the parts adjoining the land of the Idumeans,{f} and some is mountainous, the part adjoining the land of the Jews. These regions need constant attention to farming and the care of the soil, so that the people may have good harvests. This is what is done, and all of it is farmed with great abundance in the whole country I have described.

As for the cities, those of great size and a matching prosperity tend to be well populated while the countryside is neglected, since everyone is inclined toward cheerfulness of spirit, and by their very make-up all human beings are prone to pleasures.

That is what happened around Alexandria, which surpasses all cities in size and prosperity. People who came into it from the country as visitors stayed on for a long time and caused farming to decline.

So, to keep them from staying, the king ordered that no one remain as a visitor for more than twenty days. He also gave written instructions to the officials, that if it was necessary to summon anyone, they should decide the matter within five days.

He gave great weight also to the revenue officers and their assistants, and he appointed them by districts, so that the farmers and the city’s leading men, by making profit, would not run down the storehouses, I mean the produce of farming.

We have gone off on this subject because Eleazar showed us the things above so well. The industry of those who farm is great. The country is full of olive trees in large numbers, of grain crops and pulses, and also of vines and abundant honey. Other tree fruits and dates are not even counted among them.
There are many mixed herds, and abundant pasture for them. For that reason they saw rightly that the region needs a large population, and they laid out the city and the villages accordingly.

A great quantity of spices, costly stones, and gold is brought to the place through the Arabs.{g} The country is made for working and trade, the city is rich in crafts, and nothing brought by sea is lacking.

It has convenient harbors that supply it: the one at Ascalon,{h} Joppa,{i} and Gaza,{j} and also Ptolemais,{k} which the king founded. Jerusalem lies in the middle of these places and not far from them. The country has everything in abundance, well watered on every side and very secure.

The river called the Jordan,{l} which never stops flowing, runs around it. In ancient times the land measured no less than sixty million arouras (about forty million acres),{m} though later the neighbors encroached on it, and six hundred thousand men were established as landholders, each with a hundred arouras (about seventy acres). The river fills, like the Nile,{n} in the days of the harvest, and it waters much of the land.

This river sends its stream into another river in the territory of Ptolemais, and that one goes out to the sea. Other streams called torrents run down, taking in the parts toward Gaza and the land of the Azotians.{o}

The country is enclosed by natural defenses. It is hard to invade and impassable for large forces, because the approaches are narrow, with cliffs alongside and deep ravines, and the whole mountain range surrounding the entire country is rugged.

It was also said that mines of copper and iron used to be worked in the neighboring mountains of Arabia. These were abandoned in the time when the Persians ruled, because those then in charge spread the charge that working them was useless and very expensive,

so that, because of the mining of those metals, the country would not be ruined and, in effect, taken over through their power, since they would have a pretext for entering the land. I have now given you a summary of what was needed on these matters, my brother Philocrates. What concerns the translation I will explain in what follows.

Greek: “more than two talents.” A talent is taken here as about 75 pounds (34 kg).
The name Yahweh, in holy Hebrew letters, is meant.

Hebrew *Azzah*, “strong.”

Hebrew *Yarden*, “descender.”
