verses.text: For Eleazar had picked the best men, outstanding in education, since they came from distinguished parents. They had not only gained a command of the Jewish writings but had also paid serious attention to Greek learning.

For this reason they were well suited for embassies and carried them out whenever it was needed. They also had great natural ability in conversation and in discussions about the law. They pursued the middle course, which is the finest, laying aside what is rough and uncultured in the mind. Likewise they had risen above conceit and the belief that they were superior to others. They had taken up courtesy, listening, and giving each person a fitting answer. All of them kept these habits, and each wanted to outdo the others in them, and all were worthy of their leader and of his excellence.

It was easy to see how they loved Eleazar and could hardly be parted from him, and he loved them. Besides writing to the king about their return, he urged Andreas strongly to do the same, asking him to help as far as we could.

When we promised to see to this, he said that he was very anxious, for he knew that the king, who loves what is good, counts it the greatest thing of all to send for any person who is named, in whatever place, as outstanding above others in conduct and understanding.

I have learned that the king rightly says that if he has just and sensible men around him, he will have the greatest protection for his kingdom, since friends will advise him frankly for his benefit; and this is the case with those sent by him.
He also gave his oath not to let these men be used up on any other need of his own, but to send them out only for the common improvement of all the citizens.

“Living well,” he said, “lies in keeping the commandments of the law, and this is accomplished by hearing far more than by reading.” By putting forward these and similar thoughts he made plain the attitude he had toward them.

It is worth mentioning briefly what he showed us in answer to what we asked. I think that many people are curious about certain things in the legislation, about foods and drinks and the animals thought to be unclean.

We asked why, when there is a single creation, some animals are held unclean for eating and others even for touching. (The law is scrupulous in most matters, and in these it is extremely so.) He began his answer in this way.

“You see,” he said, “what effect our habits and our associations have, for when people keep company with the wicked they pick up twisted ways and are wretched through the whole of their lives. But if they live with the wise and sensible, they pass out of ignorance and find the setting right of their lives.

So our lawgiver first set out the matters of piety and justice and taught each of them, not only by forbidding but by showing, making plain both the harms and the punishments that God sends on those responsible—

for he showed first of all that God is the only God, that his power is made plain through all things, that every place is filled with his dominion, and that nothing done on earth by people in secret escapes him. Whatever anyone does is plain to him, and so are the things that will come about—

and by working these points out exactly and setting them in plain view, he showed that if anyone should even think of committing wrong, it would not go unnoticed, still less if he did it, since throughout the whole law he displays the power of God.
After this opening, having shown that all other peoples apart from us believe in many gods, though they are in themselves far stronger than the gods they worship for nothing—

for they make statues of stone and wood, and they say these are images of people who discovered something useful for living, and they bow down to them, though the lack of feeling in these things lies right at their feet.

If anyone were a god on that basis, because of an invention, it would be completely senseless. For these inventors took certain things already in creation, put them together, and showed that they were useful; they did not make the substance of them themselves. So it is empty and foolish to make gods of people like themselves.

Even now there are many people more inventive and better taught than the people of earlier times, and yet no one would be in a hurry to worship them. The Greeks who shaped these ideas and spun these tales believe themselves to be the wisest.

Why even speak of the other worthless worshipers, the Egyptians and those like them, who have trusted in wild beasts and in nearly every sort of reptile and animal, and bow down to them and sacrifice to them, both living and dead?

When our lawgiver, a wise man equipped by God for knowledge of all things, had considered each point, he fenced us in with unbroken palisades and walls of iron, so that we would not mix with any of the other nations in any way. We were to stay pure in body and soul, freed from empty beliefs, worshiping the one mighty God over the whole of creation.

For this reason the leading priests of Egypt, who have looked deeply into many things and shared in many affairs, call us “men of God.” This title does not belong to the rest, unless someone worships the God who truly is. The others are men of food and drink and shelter,
for their whole outlook takes refuge in these things. Among our people these count for nothing, and their thought is given to the dominion of God throughout the whole of life.

So that we would not be corrupted by mixing with anyone or by keeping company with the base, he fenced us in on every side with rules of purity, in accordance with the law, concerning foods and drinks and touch and hearing and sight.

In general, all things are alike by natural reason, governed by one power, and each one has a deep meaning in what we avoid using and what we do use. As an example, I will go over one or two points briefly for you.

Do not fall into the cheap view that Moses{a} made these laws out of fussiness over mice and weasels and such creatures. No: everything has been arranged with dignity, for the sake of pure inquiry and the shaping of character toward justice.
Of the birds we eat, all are tame and distinguished by their cleanness, feeding on wheat and pulses: doves, turtledoves, francolins, and partridges, and also geese and others of the kind.

As for the birds that are forbidden, you will find them wild and meat-eating, lording it over the rest by their strength, and feeding unjustly on the tame birds I have mentioned. Not only this, but they snatch up lambs and kids, and they harm people, both dead and living.

By naming these birds unclean, he set a mark on them. It showed that those for whom the law was laid down must practice justice in their souls and not lord it over anyone, trusting in their own strength, nor take anything away, but steer the affairs of life by what is right, just as the tame birds I mentioned feed on the pulses that grow on the ground and do not use their power to destroy their own kind.
Through such examples the lawgiver handed down a sign for those with understanding: to be just, to carry out nothing by force, and not to lord it over others by relying on one’s own strength.
Since he did not allow us even to touch the creatures I mentioned, because of the character of each, how could one fail to take great care that our own conduct is not bent toward such things?

So all the concessions made to us about these birds and about cattle are set out in figurative terms. For having a cloven foot, with the hoof divided into claws, is a sign of separating each action toward what is good.

The strength of the whole body, with its working power, rests on the shoulders and legs. So the sign given through these animals compels us to do everything with discrimination, toward justice. It also reminds us that we have been set apart from all other people.

Most of the rest of mankind defile themselves by their intercourse, and so commit great injustice, and whole countries and cities are proud of it. They not only take males as partners, but they also defile their own mothers and even daughters. We have been set apart from these things.

He has also stamped the mark of remembrance on the very same thing that the mode of separation concerns. For all animals that part the hoof and bring up the cud set forth, clearly for those who understand, the idea of memory.
For chewing the cud is nothing other than a recalling of life and existence, since he reckons that life is sustained by food.

That is why scripture also urges us, saying: “You shall remember well Yahweh,{b} who has done great and wonderful things in you.” For when they are looked into, these things prove great and glorious: first of all, how the body is put together, how food is handled, and the separation of each limb;

and much more, the ordering of the senses, the working of the mind and its unseen motion, the quickness to act in each matter, and the invention of crafts, all of which hold a manner beyond understanding.

So he urges us to remember that these things are kept in being by divine power along with their construction. For he has set aside every time and every place for constantly remembering the God who rules and sustains.

He commands that over food and drink we first make an offering and only then use them. Through our garments, too, he has given us a mark of remembrance, and in the same way he has ordered us to place the words on our gates and doors, as a reminder of God.
On the hands he expressly commands that the sign be fastened, showing plainly that every action must be carried out with justice, remembering our own makeup, and above all the fear of God.

He commands also that when we lie down and when we rise we think over the works of God, observing not merely in speech but by reflection the movement and perception that come over us when we go to sleep, and our waking, and how divine and beyond grasp is the change from one to the other.

You have now been shown the deeper meaning of the law about separation and remembrance, in our account of the split hoof and the chewing of the cud. These things were not laid down at random or on whatever came into the mind, but for the sake of truth and the marking out of right reasoning.

For having given instructions about foods and drinks and everything to do with touch, he commands that we do nothing and hear nothing at random, and that we not use the power of speech to turn toward injustice.
The same can be found with the animals. The way of the weasel and of creatures like it, those named in the law, is harmful.
Mice damage and harm everything, not only for their own food but so as to make completely useless to a person whatever they happen to set upon harming.
The kind of weasel is peculiar. Apart from what was said, it has a damaging nature, for it conceives by way of the ears and gives birth by way of the mouth.

For this reason such a way among people is unclean. Those who take in things by hearing and then give them a body in speech, rolling others into evil, accomplish no ordinary wrong, and they are themselves wholly polluted with the stain of impiety. Your king does well to put such people to death, as we understand.”

I said, “I suppose you mean the informers; for he keeps bringing on them torture and painful deaths.” “Those are the very ones I mean,” he said, “for keeping watch to bring about people’s ruin is unholy.

Our law orders us to do no harm to anyone, whether in word or in deed. So on these matters, too, I have shown you briefly that everything has been regulated toward justice, and that nothing in scripture has been laid down at random or as a fable. Its purpose is that through the whole of life, and in our actions, we practice justice toward all people, remembering the ruling God.
So the whole account of foods and of unclean reptiles and animals points toward justice and just dealing among people.”

It seemed to me that he defended each point well. He also said, about the offerings of calves, rams, and goats, that these must be taken from herds and flocks and be tame animals when sacrificed, and nothing wild, so that those who bring the sacrifices will be aware of nothing proud in themselves, keeping in view the sign given by the one who laid down the rule. For the person who brings the sacrifice makes the offering of his own soul, of his whole manner of life.

I think that what was said in that conversation is worth recording on these matters too. So I have gone on to explain to you, Philocrates, the dignity and natural reasoning of the law, because of your love of learning.

notes.text: Greek *Mouses*, from Hebrew *Mosheh*, “drawn out” (Exodus 2:10).
The Greek has *Kyrios*, “Lord,” the word the Greek Bible uses in place of the Hebrew name Yahweh. The words echo Deuteronomy 7:18 and 10:21.

verses.text: Eleazar offered a sacrifice, chose the men, prepared many gifts for the king, and dispatched us with a heavy escort.
When we reached Alexandria, the king was told of our arrival. Andreas and I were admitted to the court, and we greeted the king warmly and handed over the letters from Eleazar.
He placed great value on meeting the men who had been sent, and ordered every other official dismissed and the men summoned.

This struck everyone as remarkable, since the custom was that people who came on business could reach the king’s presence only on the fifth day, and envoys from kings or from important cities were barely admitted to the court within thirty. But he thought those who had come worthy of greater honor, and he judged the standing of the one who had sent them. So he dismissed those he thought unnecessary and waited, walking about, until he could greet them as they came in.

They came forward with the gifts that had been sent and the precious skins on which the law was written in gold letters in Hebrew script. The parchment was wonderfully worked, and the joins between the sheets had been made so that they could not be felt. When the king caught sight of the men, he inquired about the books.

They uncovered the wrappings and unrolled the sheets. The king stood there a long time, bowed down about seven times, and said, “I thank you, men, and the one who sent you even more, and above all God, whose words these are.”

Everyone who had come, and everyone who was present, cried out together with one voice, “Well said, O king!” Tears came to him, and he was full of joy. For the strain on the soul and the weight of such an honor force tears at moments of success.

He ordered the rolls to be put back in order. Then he greeted the men and said, “It was right, you godly men, that I first pay reverence to the books for whose sake I sent for you, and only after that hold out my right hand to you. That is why I did this first.

I count this day, on which you arrived, a great day, and it will be marked every year all the days of our life. It also happens to coincide with news of our victory in the sea battle against Antigonus.{a} So today I will want to dine with you.

Everything will be provided for you in a fitting way,” he said, “for you to use, and for me with you.” They were delighted. He ordered that the best lodgings near the citadel be given them and that the banquet be prepared.

Nicanor,{b} the chief usher, called in Dorotheus,{c} who had been put in charge of these matters, and ordered him to carry out the preparations for each person. For this was how the kings had arranged it, as you can still see today: for every city that has its own customs in drink, food, and bedding, there was an officer in charge. Preparations were made according to those customs whenever the envoys came before the kings, so that, troubled in nothing, they could pass the time cheerfully. That was done for these men too.

Dorotheus was a very careful man and had charge of such matters. He laid out everything that was handled through him, divided up for such receptions. He made the arrangement of the couches in two groups, as the king had ordered: half of the guests were to recline at his right hand, and the rest after his own couch, leaving nothing lacking in honoring the men.

When they were seated, the king told Dorotheus to proceed according to the customs followed by all who come to him from Judea. For that reason he excused the sacred heralds, the sacrificers, and the others who were accustomed to make the prayers, and he asked Elisha,{d} who had come with us and was an elder among the priests, to make the prayer. Elisha stood and spoke in a worthy way.

“O king, may God Almighty fill you with all the good things he has created. May he grant that you keep these, with your wife and children and those who share your mind, never failing, all the days of your life.”

When he had said this, applause burst out with shouting and glad joy for a long time. Then they turned to enjoy what had been prepared, with all the services carried out under Dorotheus’s direction. Among those serving were royal pages and some of those honored by the king.

notes.text: Greek *Antigonos*, perhaps “worthy of his fathers.” The sea battle is not identified with certainty.
Greek *Nikanor*, “victorious.”
Greek *Dorotheos*, “gift of God.”
Hebrew *Elisha*, “God saves.” He is the Elisha of the first tribe named in 4:4.

verses.text: When he found an opening after an interval, he asked the man on the first couch (for they were seated by age), “How could I keep my kingdom free of stumbling to the end?”

After a brief pause he said, “You would govern best by imitating God’s constant gentleness. If you practice patience and treat those who deserve it more mildly, as each deserves, you will turn them from wickedness and bring them to repentance.”

The king praised him and asked the next, “How could I do everything well?” He answered, “If you keep justice toward everyone, you will do each thing well for yourself, understanding that every thought is clear to God. If you begin from the fear of God, you will fail in nothing.”

The king gladly accepted this answer and asked another, “How could I have friends who are like myself?” He said, “If they see you taking great care of the crowds you rule. You will do this by observing the good God does for the human race, supplying health and food and everything else in due season.”

The king confirmed this and asked the next, “How could I win good reports in my business and judgments, even from those who lose their case?” He said, “If you are the same to all in what you say, and do nothing proudly or by the force of your own strength against those who do wrong.

You will do this by looking at the order God has set. Requests are granted to those who are worthy, and those who fail are shown, through dreams or events, the harm that is theirs. God does not strike them according to their sins or the greatness of his strength; he acts with gentleness.”

He praised this man well too and asked the next in order, “How could I be undefeated in the demands of war?” He said, “If you do not put your trust in crowds or forces, but call on God in everything, so that he may direct your undertakings as you carry out everything justly.”

He welcomed this man too and asked another, “How could I be feared by my enemies?” He said, “If, though you have a great supply of arms and forces, you know that these are empty and over a long time accomplish little in the end. For God, who grants respites and shows the fear of his dominion, builds it into every mind.”

He praised this man as well and said to the next, “What would be the finest thing for me in life?” He said, “To know that God is ruler of all, and that even in our finest actions it is not we who direct what we have planned. God brings everyone’s plans to completion and guides them with his power.”

He said this man too spoke well, and asked another, “How could I keep everything unharmed and hand down the same disposition to my descendants to the end?” He said, “By praying always to God to receive good thoughts for what is to be done, and by urging your descendants not to be dazzled by fame or riches. For these are granted by God, and they do not hold their supremacy over everything by their own doing.”

He confirmed this and asked the one after him, “How could I bear what happens with moderation?” He said, “If you accept in advance that God made all people to share in the greatest evils as well as in goods, and that no human being can be free from a mixture of them. God gives courage, and he must be asked for it.”

He welcomed this man too, and said that everyone was answering well. “I will ask one more and then stop for now, so that we may turn to pleasure and pass the time agreeably. In the next six days, one after another, I will learn something more from the rest.”

Then he asked the man, “What does courage aim at?” He said, “That what has been rightly planned be carried out as intended in the actions of danger. And God brings everything to completion for you, O king, since you plan well and to good purpose.”

Everyone cheered and signaled their approval with applause. The king said to the philosophers (not a few were present with them), “These men, I think, stand out in virtue and have greater understanding, since, though given such questions on the spur of the moment, they answered as they should, all of them making God the starting point of their discourse.”

Menedemus{a} of Eretria,{b} a philosopher, said, “Yes, O king. All things are governed by providence, and they have rightly assumed that man is God’s creation, so it follows that all power and all beauty of speech begin with God.”
The king nodded, the discussion of these matters ended, and they turned to merriment. When evening came, the banquet broke up.

On the next day the reclining and the drinking went on in the same arrangement. When the king thought it a good time to ask the men something, he questioned those who came next after the ones who had answered the day before.
He began the conversation with the eleventh, for ten had been questioned the day before. When there was silence, he asked, “How could one stay rich?”

After a short pause, the one who received the question said, “If he does nothing unworthy of himself or dissolute, if he does not spend on empty and vain things, and if he wins those under him to goodwill by kindness. For God is the cause of good things for all, and one must follow him.”

The king praised this man and asked another, “How could one keep to the truth?” He answered, “By knowing that a lie brings great shame on everyone, and much more on kings. Since they have authority to do what they want, why would they lie? You must also take this in, O king: God loves truth.”

He welcomed this man too, looked at the next, and said, “What does the teaching of wisdom consist of?” The other declared, “As you do not want evils to come to yourself but want a share in all good things, so you ought to deal with your subjects and with those who do wrong, and admonish the good and noble among people rather gently. For God leads all people with gentleness.”

He praised him and said to the next, “How could one be kind to people?” He said, “By observing that the human race grows and is born over a long time and with the greatest suffering. So one should not punish readily or heap abuse on people, knowing that human life is made of pains and penalties. If you think over each case, you will turn toward mercy, for God is merciful.”

He welcomed this man and put to the next man this question: “What does a kingdom need most?” “To keep oneself free of bribes,” he said, “to be sober for most of one’s life, to put justice first, and to make friends of such people. For God loves justice.”

He took note of this and turned to another: “What does piety consist of?” He said, “To understand that God is at work and aware of everything at every moment, and that no one who commits an injustice or an evil could escape him. As God benefits the whole world, so you also, if you imitate him, would be free from stumbling.”

He applauded this and said to another, “What is the limit of ruling?” He said, “To rule oneself well, and, not being carried away by wealth and glory, to desire nothing proud or unseemly, if you reason well. For everything is at your command as if it were nothing. God needs nothing and is gentle. You too, so far as you are human, should keep this in mind, and not reach for many things, but for what suffices for ruling.”

He praised him and asked another, “How could one best deliberate?” He answered, “If he constantly puts justice before everything and considers injustice a loss of life. For God always foretells the greatest good for the just.”

He praised this man and said to the next, “How could one be untroubled in sleep?” He said, “You have asked a thing that is hard to explain. We cannot keep ourselves in hand in what happens in sleep, but are held by a perception that does not reason.

In the soul we are affected by what comes upon us as if we were really seeing it. We lose our reason, in that we suppose we are out on the open sea in ships, or flying through the air and carried off to other places, and other things of the kind, and the one who supposes these things does not stand firm.{c}

Still, as far as I can reach it, I have understood it this way. In every way, O king, bring both what is said and what is done back to piety, so that you are conscious that, keeping to virtue, you choose neither to show favor against reason nor, using your authority, to set aside what is just.

In most cases, the matters in which each person passes the time while awake are the same ones in which the mind dwells during sleep. And a person who directs all reasoning and action toward what is finest does so awake and asleep. For that reason steadiness is always with you.”
He praised this man warmly and said to the other, “Since you are the tenth to give an answer, once you have spoken we will turn to the dinner.”

He asked, “How could we do nothing unworthy of ourselves?” He said, “Keep your eye always on your own reputation and eminence, so that you speak and think in keeping with them, knowing that all those you rule think and talk about you.

For you must not appear the least of the actors. The role they must play, they watch carefully and do everything to match it. But you are not playing a part; you truly reign, since God has given you rule that suits your character.”
The king applauded him warmly and with great friendliness for a long time, and then the men were urged to go and sleep. When this was finished, they went on to the next day’s banquet.

On the following day the same arrangement was followed, and when the king thought it a good time to ask the men something, he asked the first of those who remained for the next question: “What is the strongest rule?”
He said, “To rule oneself and not be swept along by one’s impulses. For in every person the mind naturally leans toward something.

Most people are likely to be inclined toward food, drink, and pleasures; kings, toward the conquest of territory, in keeping with the greatness of their glory. But moderation in everything is good. Take what God gives and hold on to it; do not desire what is out of reach.”

notes.text: Greek *Menedemos*, “staying with the people.”
Greek *Eretria*, a city on the island of Euboea, perhaps “city of rowers.”
The Greek of this verse is damaged, and the sense is uncertain.

verses.text: Pleased with what had been said, he asked the next, “How could one be free of envy?” After a pause he said, “First, if he understood that God apportions glory and great wealth to kings, and that no one is king by his own doing. All people want a share in this glory, but they cannot have it, for it is God’s gift.”

He praised the man at some length and asked another, “How could one look down on his enemies?” He said, “If you have practiced goodwill toward all people and built up friendships, you would take no one into account. To be well liked by all and to have received this fine gift from God is the strongest protection.”

He agreed with this and told the next to answer, asking, “How could one keep a good reputation?” He said, “By being generous and open-handed to others, with eagerness and kindness, you would never lose your reputation. And so that what I have said may last for you, call on God always.”

He praised him and asked another, “How should one show a love of honor?” He said, “Everyone thinks one should show it to those who are friendly to us. I suppose we should show a gracious generosity above all toward those who think differently, so that we may thereby lead them to what is fitting and to their own advantage. One must pray to God that this be accomplished, for he controls the minds of all.”

He agreed with this and told the sixth to give his view, asking, “Whom should one show favor to?” He answered, “To parents always, for God has made the greatest commandment about honoring parents. Next he approves devotion to friends, calling a friend equal to one’s own soul. You do well to bring all people into friendship with you.”

He encouraged this man and asked the next after him, “What is worthy of being called beauty?” He said, “Piety. For this is a kind of beauty that takes first place, and its power is love, which is God’s gift. You too possess it, with all good things contained in it.”

He applauded most warmly and said to another, “How could one who has stumbled win back the same reputation?” He said, “It is not possible for you to stumble, since you have sown kindnesses among all people, and these sprout goodwill, which is stronger than the greatest weapons and carries the greatest security.
If some do stumble, they must no longer do the things at which they stumble, but win friendship and act justly. To be a doer of good, and not of the opposite, is God’s gift.”
He was pleased with this and said to the next, “How could one be free of grief?” He said, “If he harms no one but helps everyone, following justice. For its fruits produce freedom from grief.

One must also beg God to keep from harming us what comes up against our own choice. I mean such things as death, sickness, griefs, and the like. As for you, since you are pious, none of these will come near you.”

He praised this man too, and asked the tenth, “What is greatest in glory?” He said, “Honoring God. This is done by neither gifts nor sacrifices, but by a pure soul and a holy understanding, that all things are made and governed by God according to his will. You have always held this view, and it can be seen by everyone from what you have accomplished and are accomplishing.”

Raising his voice, the king welcomed them all and urged them on, and those present joined in the cheers, especially the philosophers. For the visitors were far ahead of them in conduct and speech, since they made God their starting point. After that the king went on to show his friendliness by proposing toasts.

On the next day the banquet followed the same arrangement. When the moment suited the king, he put his questions to those who followed the men already answered. He said to the first, “Can understanding be taught?” He said, “It is the makeup of the soul, through divine power, to take in everything fine and to turn away from the opposite.”
He agreed and asked the next, “What contributes most to health?” He said, “Self-control. It cannot be gained unless God shapes the mind toward it.”

He encouraged this man and said to another, “How could one repay parents with the thanks they deserve?” He said, “By causing them no grief. That cannot be unless God leads the mind to the finest things.”

He nodded to this and asked the next, “How could one be a good listener?” He said, “By understanding that it is useful to know everything, so that when events come, one may choose something of what he has heard and set it against the circumstances of the moment, with God’s hand to guide him. That is to say, the accomplishment of one’s actions comes from God.”

He praised this man and said to another, “How could one do nothing against the law?” He said, “By knowing that God gave the ideas to the lawmakers to preserve the lives of people, you would follow them.”

He welcomed this man and said to another, “What is the benefit of kinship?” He declared, “If, when misfortune comes on our relatives, we count ourselves diminished and suffer as if it were ourselves, then the strength of kinship appears.{a}

When this is done, glory and progress will be found among such people. For help given with goodwill, as if from oneself, cannot be dissolved by anything, and in good times there is no need of anything from them. But one must pray to God, who makes everything good.”

In the same way he welcomed this man and asked another, “How does fearlessness come about?” He said, “When the mind is aware that it has done nothing wrong, and God directs it to deliberate well in everything.”

He applauded this and said to another, “How could one keep right reason ready at hand?” He said, “If he always keeps in view the misfortunes of people, knowing that God takes away prosperity and raises up others to be honored.”

He welcomed this man too, and asked the next to answer, “How could one avoid turning to ease and pleasures?” He said, “By keeping in mind that he rules a great kingdom and leads many crowds, and that his thoughts should be on nothing else but the care of them. And by asking God that none of his duties be neglected.”

He praised this man, the tenth, and asked, “How could one recognize those who act toward him with some deceit?” He declared, “By watching whether their conduct is free and whether good order holds in their greetings, in their counsel, and in the rest of their dealings with those around him, and whether they overdo nothing beyond what is right in friendliness and in the rest of their behavior.
God will lead your mind to the finest things, O king.” The king applauded them all and praised each by name, and those present did the same. Then they turned to song.

On the next day, finding the occasion, he put a question to the next, “What is the greatest neglect?” He said, “If someone is careless about his children and does not strive to bring them up in every way. We always pray to God, less for ourselves than for our descendants, that every good thing may be theirs. That children come to share in self-control happens by God’s power.”

He said this man spoke well and asked another, “How could one be a lover of his country?” He said, “By setting it before himself that it is good to live, and also to die, in one’s own country. Living abroad brings contempt on the poor and shame on the rich, as if they had been driven out for wickedness. By doing good to all, as you constantly do, since God gives you favor with all, you will appear a lover of your country.”

He listened to him and asked the following man, “How should one get along with a wife?” He said, “By knowing that the female sex is bold, and energetic in whatever it wants, and easily turned by faulty reasoning, and by nature made weak. One must treat her sensibly and not oppose her in quarrels.
For life is steered rightly when the one at the helm knows to what goal the course must be made. And by calling on God, life is steered rightly in everything.”

He agreed with this man and asked the next, “How could one be without fault?” He said, “By doing everything with careful thought and not believing slanders, but being yourself the tester of what is said, directing the matters brought before you by judgment, and carrying them out by judgment. In that way you would be without fault, O king. To devise such things and to live by them is the work of divine power.”

He was delighted by what was said and asked another, “How could one be free of anger?” He said, “By knowing that he has authority over all, and that if he gave way to anger he would bring death, which is useless and painful if the life of many is taken away because he is lord. When all are subject and no one is opposing, why would he be angry?
One must know that God governs the whole world with kindness and without any anger. You must follow him, O king.”

He said this man had answered well and asked the one after, “What is good counsel?” He declared, “To do everything well with careful thought, setting out in the planning the harmful things on the opposite side of the argument, so that when we have thought through each one, we may be well advised and what was proposed may be carried out. And best of all, by God’s power every plan will reach its completion for you as you practice piety.”

He said this man too had done well and asked another, “What is philosophy?” He declared, “To reason well about each thing that happens and not be carried away by impulses, but to study the harms that come out of desires, and to do what suits the moment in a properly measured way. To gain a firm grasp of these things, we must serve God.”

He marked this answer and asked another, “How could one win acceptance as a stranger in a foreign land?” He said, “By being equal to everyone, and appearing to be lesser rather than greater than those among whom he is a stranger. For in general God welcomes what is humble according to nature, and the human race is kind to those who submit.”

He affirmed these answers and asked another, “How could what one builds last afterward?” He said, “If he makes great and dignified works, so that those who see them spare them for their beauty; if he sends away none of those who work on them; and if he does not force others to do the needed work without pay.

By thinking that God cares for the human race, providing them with health and keen senses and the rest, he will himself do something fitting, paying back the reward for their labors. What is done in justice is also what lasts.”
Saying that this man also spoke well, he questioned the tenth: “What does wisdom yield?” He said, “Not to be aware of having done any wrong, and to pass one’s life in truth.

From these, the greatest joy and steadiness of soul come to you, O greatest of kings, and good hopes in God, as you hold your rule with piety.” When all heard this, they cheered with louder applause. After this the king, filled with joy, turned to the toasts.

On the next day the arrangements for the drinking went as before, and when the moment came, the king put questions to those who were left. To the first he said, “How could one avoid turning to pride?”
He answered, “If he keeps equality and reminds himself in each case that, though a man, he rules over men. God brings down the proud and lifts up the gentle and humble.”

He encouraged him and put a question to the next: “Which counselors should one use?” “Those who have been tested through many affairs,” he said, “and who keep their goodwill toward him unspoiled, and all who share his ways. God shows himself to the worthy in such matters.”

He praised him and turned to another: “What must a king possess above all?” “The kindness and love of those under him,” he answered. “For through these an unbreakable bond of goodwill comes about. That these arise by choice, God brings about.”

He praised him highly and questioned another, “What is the goal of speech?” He said, “To persuade the one who disagrees, by showing the harms through an ordered series of points. In this way you will win the listener not by opposing him but by using praise to persuade. Persuasion is directed by God’s working.”

He said this man spoke well and asked another, “How could one get along with the crowds of every kind in the kingdom?” “By playing the fitting part with each,” he said, “taking justice as your guide, as you do, since God gives you the ability to reason well.”

He was pleased with this and said to another, “What should one grieve over?” He answered, “What happens to friends, when we see it become long-lasting and inescapable. When they have died and are released from evils, reason does not call for grief. But people refer things back to themselves and to what concerns them, and so all people grieve. To escape every evil comes by God’s power.”

He said that this man had answered as he should, and said to another, “How does dishonor come about?” He said, “When pride leads, and boldness that never stops, contempt grows up with them, and the loss of glory. God is lord of all glory, and tips it where he wishes.”

He confirmed this answer too and asked the next, “Whom should one trust?” “Those who are with you out of goodwill,” he said, “and not out of fear or for the sake of attention, bringing everything round to profit. The one is a sign of love; the other, of ill will and opportunism, for whoever is driven by greed is born a traitor. You have well-wishers all around you, since God gives you good counsel.”

verses.text: He encouraged this man and asked another, “What preserves favor and honor?” He said, “Virtue. For it is the accomplishment of fine works and drives off evil. You keep up your nobility toward everyone, having it as a gift from God.”

He received this man warmly too and asked the eleventh (for there were two more than seventy),{a} “How could one be at peace in spirit even in wars?” He declared, “By understanding that he has done no wrong to anyone under him, and that all will struggle on behalf of his benefactions, knowing that even if they depart from life, you are the caretaker of their lives.

For you never cease setting everyone right, since God has given you good sense.” The king marked their approval with applause and welcomed them all warmly. Toasting each one at greater length, he turned to enjoyment, keeping company with the men in cheer and great joy.

On the seventh of the days, with greater preparation made and many more arriving from the cities (for there were a good number of envoys), the king, when the occasion came, asked the leader of those who remained to be questioned, “How could one avoid being led astray by false reasoning?”

He said, “By testing the speaker, and what is said, and what it is about, and by asking the same things over a longer time in different ways. A keen mind, able to judge each matter, is a fine gift of God, and you have it, O king.”

The king marked his approval with applause and asked another, “Why do most people not accept virtue?” “Because all people are by nature lacking in self-control and have turned toward pleasures,” he said. “From this injustice grows, and the flood of greed.
The state of virtue holds back those who are carried toward indulgence, and orders them to put self-control and justice first. And God leads in all of these.”

The king said this man had answered well and asked, “What should kings follow?” He said, “The laws, so that through just actions they may rebuild people’s lives. By doing this you have laid down a memorial of yourself that will never fade, following a divine command.”

Saying this man had also spoken well, he asked the next, “Who should be made a general?” He said, “Those who hate evil, who imitate your conduct so as always to be well thought of, and who do what is just. This is what you do, greatest of kings, since God has given you a crown of justice.”

He welcomed him aloud, looked at the next, and said, “Whom should one set over the armies as commanders?” He declared, “Those who excel in courage and justice, who think much more of saving their men than of winning, and who risk their own lives in daring. As God does good to all, you too, imitating him, do good to those under you.”

The king said this man had answered well and asked another, “What kind of person is worth admiring?” He said, “One who is supplied with glory, wealth, and power and yet is equal to all in spirit. You are admirable in doing this, since God gives you the care for such things.”

He applauded this man too and said to another, “What should kings occupy themselves with for most of their time?” He said, “With reading, and with studying the reports of missions and journeys, whatever has been written about kingdoms to set people right and keep them safe. In doing this you have gained a glory that others cannot reach, since God brings your wishes to completion.”

He addressed this man too with energy and asked another, “What pastimes should one choose in times of relaxation and ease?” He said, “To watch whatever is played out with restraint, and to set before one’s eyes the things of life that are done with propriety and decorum. For even in these there is some benefit.
Often even from the smallest things something worth choosing is shown. You, having practiced every kind of restraint, philosophize through your actions out of nobility, and are honored by God.”

He was pleased with what had been said and asked the ninth, “How should one spend banquets?” He said, “By inviting those who love learning and are able to remind one of what benefits the kingdom and the lives of those who are ruled. You would find nothing more harmonious or more musical than these.
For such people are dear to God, having trained their minds toward the finest things. You do this too, since everything is directed for you by God.”

He was delighted with this and asked the next, “Which is better for the crowds: to have as king over them one who was a private citizen, or one born of a king?” He said, “The one who is best by nature.

For kings born of kings become savage and harsh toward their subjects. And even more, some private citizens who have known evils and shared in poverty have, once they ruled crowds, turned out harsher than godless tyrants.

But as I said, a good character that has had a share in education is able to rule. So you are a great king, not so much for the glory of your rule and wealth as for the fact that in gentleness and kindness you surpass all people, since God has given you these.”

He praised this man too for a long time and asked the last of all, “What is greatest in a kingdom?” He said, “That those under him always live in peace, and that justice is quickly obtained in the courts.

These come about through the leader, when he hates evil and loves good and values highly the saving of a human life. You too have regarded injustice as the greatest evil, and by governing everything justly you have built up a reputation that will not fade, since God has given you a mind that is pure and unmixed with any evil.”

When he had finished, applause burst out with shouting and joy for a long while. When it stopped, the king took a cup and drank a toast to all who were present and to the words that had been spoken. Before them all he said, “The greatest good has come to me through your coming.

I have been helped in many ways, since you have laid down teaching for me on how to rule.” He ordered three talents of silver{b} to be given to each one, and an attendant to take him back to his quarters. When all cheered, the banquet was filled with joy, and the king, without pause, turned to cheerfulness.

About 225 pounds (102 kilograms) of silver for each man. The Greek says three *talents*, at about 75 pounds each.

verses.text: Forgive me, Philocrates, if I have said too much on these matters. I admired the men beyond what was needed, since they gave on the spot answers that would have needed a great deal of time.

The questioner had thought through each point, and the answerers matched their replies to his questions. To me they seemed deserving of wonder, and so to those present, above all the philosophers. I think the record will seem unbelievable to all who take it up.

To lie about what is recorded is not fitting, and if I strayed at all, it would be unholy in matters like these. What happened is what we set out, keeping clear of every error. That is why, after I had accepted the force of their speech, I tried to get from the recorders each of the things that were done in the king’s audiences and at the banquets.
For it is the custom, as you also know, that from the day the king starts his business until he lies down to sleep, everything said and done is written down, and this is a good and useful practice.
On the next day, what was done and said the day before is read aloud before the business begins, and if anything was done improperly, the act is corrected.
So I got everything accurately from the records, as I have said, and have set it down, knowing your love of learning for what is useful.

After three days Demetrius took them, crossed the sea-wall of seven stadia{a} that runs out to the island,{b} crossed the bridge, and went on toward the northern part. He held a meeting in a house prepared by the shore, splendid and set in great stillness, and urged the men to complete the translation, with everything needed provided.
They carried out each part, making their versions agree with one another by comparing them. What came out of the agreement was properly written down by Demetrius.
The sessions went on until the ninth hour,{c} and after that the men were released to care for their bodies, with everything they chose provided in abundance.

Besides this, Dorotheus also provided every day everything that was prepared for the king, since he had been ordered to by the king. At dawn each day they came to the court, and after greeting the king they went back to their own place.
As is the custom of all the Jews, they washed their hands in the sea so that they could pray to God, and then turned to reading and explaining each passage.

I asked this too: “Why do they pray after washing their hands?” They explained that it is a witness that they have done no evil, since every action is carried out through the hands. They were transferring everything, nobly and piously, to justice and truth.

As we said before, they gathered each day at that place, which was pleasant for its quiet and brightness, and completed the task set. And so it happened that the translation was finished in seventy-two days, as though it had been planned that way.

When it was completed, Demetrius gathered the Jewish community at the place where the translation had been finished and read it to everyone, with the translators present. They also received great approval from the crowd, as men who had brought about great good.
In the same way they welcomed Demetrius and urged him to give the whole law, now translated, to their leaders.

When the scrolls had been read, the priests, the elders of the translators, those from the community, and the leaders of the crowd stood and said, “Since it has been translated well and piously and with precision in every respect, it is right that it remain as it is and that no alteration be made.”

All agreed. As is their custom, they ordered a curse on anyone who altered it by adding anything, changing any part of what was written, or removing anything. They did this rightly, so that it would always be kept lasting and unchanged.

When this was reported to the king, he rejoiced greatly, for the purpose he had held seemed to have been safely accomplished. All of it was read to him, and he was amazed at the thought of the lawgiver. He asked Demetrius, “Why is it that, though such great matters were accomplished, none of the historians or poets set out to mention them?”
Demetrius said, “Because the legislation is sacred and came through God. Some who tried were struck by God and gave up the attempt.

I heard from Theopompus{d} that when he was about to include in his history some of the things already translated from the law, rather rashly, his mind was disturbed for more than thirty days. In a lull he pleaded with God, and it became clear to him why this was happening.
It was shown to him in a dream that he wanted to pry into divine matters and carry them out to common people. After he held back, he recovered.

I also learned from Theodectes,{e} the tragic poet, that when he was about to bring something recorded in the book into a play, his eyes went blind with cataract. He suspected that this had happened to him for that reason, appeased God, and after many days recovered.”
When the king, as I said, had learned these things from Demetrius, he bowed in reverence and gave orders that the books be guarded with great care and kept pure.

He urged the translators to come to him more often if they returned to Judea. It was right, he said, that he send them off, and when they came, as was proper, they would have him as a friend and would receive the greatest attention from him.

He ordered their departure to be prepared, and showed the men great generosity. He gave each of them three of the finest robes, two talents of gold,{f} a cup worth a talent,{g} and a complete set of furnishings for a dining room with three couches.

He also sent to Eleazar, along with their escort, ten couches with silver feet and all their equipment, a cup worth thirty talents,{h} ten robes, purple cloth, a splendid crown, a hundred bolts of fine linen, and bowls, dishes, and two golden mixing bowls for dedication.

He wrote also to urge that if any of the men chose to come back to him, Eleazar should not stop them. He valued the company of educated men and wished to spend his wealth lavishly on such people and not on vain things.

You, Philocrates, as I promised, now have the account. I think it will please you more than the books of the myth-tellers, for you lean toward the study of things that can benefit the mind, and spend most of your time on them. I will try to write down the rest of what is noteworthy as well, so that as you go through it you may carry off the finest prize of your wish.
